sections.skill: Decide whether a task needs prediction or generation

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: A school wants each incoming email marked "absence," "question" or "other." Which kind of AI use is this?

choices.text: Predictive: it produces a label
Generative: it writes new emails
Generative: it creates new categories each day
Neither; labeling emails cannot use AI

questions.intro: Two broad uses of AI are easy to confuse. PREDICTIVE (or classifying) uses produce a LABEL or a NUMBER about the input: "spam or not spam," "92 percent likely to be a cat," "about 30 minutes." GENERATIVE uses produce NEW CONTENT: a paragraph, a picture, a song, a block of code. They fail differently. A prediction can be the wrong label or a number that is off. Generated content can look polished while containing false facts, invented details or material too close to someone else's work. Before using AI, ask: do I need a label or a number, or do I need new content?
questions.feedback: Assigning a category is a predictive (classifying) use.

sections.skill: Tell a label or number from new content

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: Which output is a label?

choices.text: A photo of a sunset
"Approved"
A three-paragraph essay
A new song melody

questions.intro: A useful skill is looking at an OUTPUT and asking what kind it is. A LABEL names a category: "spam," "cat," "approved." A NUMBER measures or predicts something: "42 minutes," "12 percent chance." NEW CONTENT is something made that did not exist before: an essay, a photo, a melody, a joke. Some outputs combine kinds: "Spam (95 percent sure)" is a label plus a number, but it is still not new content. If the output could be checked by asking "which category?" or "how much?", it is a label or a number.
questions.feedback: "Approved" names a category.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Handle tasks that mix prediction and generation

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: A help desk tool labels a billing question as "shipping," then drafts a confident reply about delivery times. What went wrong?

choices.text: The wrong label led to a confidently wrong draft
The label was right, but the draft was too short
Generators can never write help desk replies
The draft was right; billing and shipping are the same

questions.correct_answer: The wrong label led to a confidently wrong draft
questions.intro: Many real tasks mix the two uses. A help desk might first PREDICT which category a question belongs to, then GENERATE a draft reply. A mistake in the first step can make the second step confidently wrong. Some tasks are better kept predictive even when a generator could do them: if you need a yes or no answer, a confidence score and an audit trail, a classifier is easier to test than free text. And when facts matter, generated content needs checking against a source, because polished wording is not evidence.
questions.feedback: An early prediction error spread into the generated reply.
